title: Sustainable development

definition.text: Sustainable development is an approach to growth and human development that aims to meet present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet theirs.

facts.text: The widely used definition comes from the 1987 Brundtland Report, Our Common Future, which stresses the essential needs of the world's poor and the limits technology and social organisation place on the environment.
It tries to balance economic development, environmental protection and social well-being.
Its roots lie in 17th- and 18th-century European ideas of sustainable forest management, such as von Carlowitz's sustained-yield forestry.
The 1992 Earth Summit in Rio began the Rio Process that put sustainable development on the international agenda.
It is the foundational concept of the 17 Sustainable Development Goals adopted by all UN members in 2015.
Critics ask what exactly is to be sustained, and argue that no use of a non-renewable resource can be sustainable since any extraction eventually exhausts a finite stock.
The debate assumes societies manage economic, social and natural capital, which may not substitute for one another and whose use may be irreversible.

contested_note: Scholars understand the concept in many ways and criticise it from several angles, including what is to be sustained.

definition.text: The three dimensions of sustainability are the environmental, social and economic areas that scholars usually distinguish within the concept.

facts.text: Writers also call them pillars, components, aspects or goals; all mean the same here.
The familiar three-circle Venn diagram first appeared in a 1987 article by the economist Edward Barbier.
The paradigm has few theoretical foundations, though it dominates the literature.
Agenda 21 (1992) and Agenda 2030 (2015) both frame sustainability through economic, social and environmental dimensions.

definition.text: The nested model ranks the three dimensions of sustainability, drawing the economy inside society and society inside the environment.

facts.text: Many publications treat the environmental dimension, ecological or planetary integrity, as the most important, so it sets limits on economic and social development.
The SDG 'wedding cake' model likewise shows the economy as a subset of society, and society as a subset of the biosphere.
A 2022 assessment argued the SDGs fail to make protecting planetary integrity an end in itself.

title: Economic dimension of sustainability

definition.text: The economic dimension of sustainability concerns how economic development fits with protecting the environment and meeting basic needs, and it is controversial.

facts.text: The controversy arises because 'development' can be read as just economic growth, which can promote a system bad for the environment.
Economic development can reduce hunger and energy poverty, which is why SDG 8 calls for growth, measured partly by real GDP per capita.
The challenge is to expand economic activity while cutting its environmental impact.
The Brundtland Report holds that poverty both causes and results from environmental problems.

contested_note: Sources disagree whether economic growth belongs in sustainability or undermines it.

definition.text: Sustainability barriers are the reasons sustainability is so hard to achieve.

facts.text: Intrinsic barriers come from nature's complexity and the human condition, such as the value-action gap, where people do not act on their convictions.
Extrinsic barriers can be overcome, for example by putting a price on the consumption of public goods.
Competitive market economies carry a structural imperative to grow, which inhibits needed change.
Political pressure favours the short term over the long term.

definition.text: A sustainability transition (or transformation) is a deep, system-wide change in technology, economy, society, values and goals towards sustainability.

facts.text: It must happen at every scale, from local communities to global governance institutions.
It is politically debated, since stakeholders may disagree on goals and methods and it can challenge existing power and resource distribution.
It may only work if far-reaching lifestyle changes accompany technological advances.

definition.text: Daly's operational principles are three rules for sustainable development published by Herman Daly in 1990.

facts.text: Renewable resources should be harvested no faster than they regenerate, giving a sustainable yield.
Use of non-renewable resources should be matched by equivalent development of renewable substitutes.
Waste generation should not exceed the environment's assimilative capacity.
An unsustainable situation arises when natural capital is used up faster than it can be replenished.

title: Weak and strong sustainability

definition.text: Weak and strong sustainability are two opposing approaches from environmental economics that differ on whether natural capital can be replaced by human-made capital.

facts.text: Weak sustainability treats natural and human capital as interchangeable, so losing natural capital is acceptable if human capital rises by at least as much.
Strong sustainability holds that some natural assets have critical ecological functions no human-made alternative can replace, so they must be kept regardless of gains elsewhere.
Example: under weak sustainability, replacing a natural forest with a park or farmland can count as sustainable if its value equals the biodiversity lost; under strong sustainability it may not.
Pearce, Markandya and Barbier's Blueprint for a Green Economy (1989) was among the first works to discuss the ideas.
Since the 1990s there has been a heated debate over how far natural and human-made capital can substitute for each other.
Wilfred Beckerman rejects both: weak sustainability is 'redundant and illogical', and strong sustainability a 'morally repugnant and totally impracticable objective'.

contested_note: Economists actively dispute how far natural and human-made capital can substitute for each other.

title: Weak sustainability
article: Weak and strong sustainability#Weak sustainability in practice

definition.text: Weak sustainability is the view that natural capital may decline as long as human-made capital grows enough to keep the total capital stock from falling.

facts.text: It rests on the work of Robert Solow and John Hartwick, who held that human capital can substitute for natural capital.
It began in the 1970s as an extension of neoclassical growth theory that counted non-renewable resources as a factor of production, and entered the mainstream in the 1990s.
Under it, degrading the ozone layer, tropical forests or coral reefs could count as sustainable if accompanied by gains such as financial profits.
Pearce and Atkinson's measure judged most industrialised countries, and Japan with its high saving rate, sustainable, which critics see as a flaw.
Critics add that it can leave regions very sensitive to natural or economic shocks, weakening resilience.
It may be popular with governments and business but does not ensure the preservation of the Earth's ecological integrity.

contested_note: Critics argue its capital-based measures wrongly rate resource-intensive economies as sustainable.

title: Strong sustainability
article: Weak and strong sustainability#Strong sustainability argument

definition.text: Strong sustainability is the view that natural and human-made capital are complementary but not interchangeable, so certain natural capital must be preserved.

facts.text: It holds that the environment performs some functions humans and human-made capital cannot duplicate, such as the ozone layer's protection.
It puts ecological scale ahead of economic gain and treats nature as borrowed, to be passed on intact to the next generation.
One version defines and respects hard limits tied to planetary boundaries, giving some environmental changes incommensurable value.
Examples of irreplaceable functions include biodiversity, pollination, fertile soils, clean air and water, and climate regulation.

title: Capital approach to sustainability
article: Weak and strong sustainability#Capital approach to sustainability and intergenerational equity

definition.text: The capital approach judges sustainability by the stock of capital (human, natural and other) that each generation passes on.

facts.text: It gives decision makers a way to assess whether intergenerational equity, a fair distribution of assets between generations, is achieved.
Development counts as sustainable when it leaves the capital stock at least unchanged.
Human capital (skills, knowledge) and natural capital (minerals, water) are the most cited kinds of capital.
Critics note the difficulty of putting the many functions of the natural world into monetary terms.

title: Genuine savings
article: Weak and strong sustainability#Role of governance and policy recommendations

definition.text: Genuine savings is a monetary measure of a nation's net change in produced, natural and human capital stocks.

facts.text: Pearce, Atkinson and Hamilton built it on Hartwick's rule as a measure of net investment in capital.
Under weak sustainability, governance should aim to keep genuine savings at or above zero.
The World Bank and others have estimated it for many countries, and a positive value is linked to possible long-run sustainability.

title: Social bequest approach
article: Weak and strong sustainability#Rejection of both weak and strong models

definition.text: The social bequest approach reframes sustainability around what specific rights and opportunities we leave to future generations, rather than how much.

facts.text: It aims to escape a 'zero-sum' game in which present gains are automatic losses for future generations.
Daniel Bromley's rainforest example: using 25% of what remains at each decision would eventually use up the forest.

definition.text: The Brundtland Commission, formally the World Commission on Environment and Development, was a UN body set up to unite countries in pursuit of sustainable development.

facts.text: It was founded in 1983 with former Norwegian Prime Minister Gro Harlem Brundtland as chair, and dissolved in 1987 after releasing Our Common Future.
Its report popularised 'sustainable development' and gave the most widely used definition: development meeting present needs without compromising future generations' ability to meet theirs.
It responded to the conflict between globalised economic growth and accelerating ecological degradation by redefining economic development as sustainable development.
Its definition centres on the needs of the global poor and on limits technology and social organisation place on the environment, ideas close to intergenerational equity.
Its call for an international meeting led to the 1992 Rio summit and Agenda 21.
The definition's openness won wide support but was also criticised as 'self-defeating and compromised rhetoric'.

title: Hartwick's rule

definition.text: Hartwick's rule states how much a society must invest in produced capital to exactly offset the decline of its non-renewable resources, so living standards do not fall.

facts.text: Often summed up as 'invest resource rents', it requires a nation to invest all the rent earned from exhaustible resources it currently extracts.
Solow (1974) showed that, if produced capital can partly substitute for natural resources, accumulating capital fast enough can offset a shrinking resource stock.
It is the main theoretical and practical route for putting weak sustainability into governance.
The rule extends to many capital types, and the net of investment over disinvestment is called genuine savings.
Clive Spash criticised its 'self-evident lack of realism', since it treats man-made capital as not depreciating and as substituting for, not complementing, natural capital.

contested_note: Ecological economists such as Clive Spash reject its assumptions about substituting capital for nature.

definition.text: Intergenerational equity is the idea of fairness or justice between generations, including between people alive now and future generations.

facts.text: It is applied to environmental concerns such as sustainable development and climate change; depleting natural resources will likely burden future generations.
Younger cohorts will disproportionately bear environmental damage: children born in 2020 may face up to seven times as many extreme weather events as people born decades earlier.
From a weak sustainability view, it is met if environmental losses for future generations are offset by greater economic gains.
From a strong sustainability view, no amount of economic progress justifies leaving future generations a degraded environment.
Some weak-sustainability adherents put a discount rate on outcomes for future generations.
The Haudenosaunee Confederacy weighed decisions by the principle of seven generation sustainability.
In investment management, James Tobin set out in 1974 that an endowment's spending must not exceed its after-inflation return, preserving equity among generations.

definition.text: The Cobb–Douglas production function is a widely used mathematical form linking the amounts of inputs, especially labour and capital, to the output they can produce.

facts.text: Charles Cobb and Paul Douglas developed and tested it against statistical evidence between 1927 and 1947.
In its common form the exponents α and β, each between 0 and 1, are the labour and capital elasticities of output; with α = 0.45, 1% more labour gives about 0.45% more output.
It obeys diminishing returns: each extra unit of a factor raises output, but by less and less.
Its elasticity of substitution between inputs is constant and equal to 1.
If the exponents sum to 1 returns to scale are constant; below 1 decreasing; above 1 increasing.
It is the limiting case of the CES production function as its substitution parameter goes to zero.
Critics fault its lack of foundation and its assumption of a constant labour share of output, which is now widely seen to be declining.

definition.text: Constant elasticity of substitution (CES) is a common form for production and utility functions in which the ease of substituting one input or good for another stays the same at all levels of output or utility.

facts.text: The two-factor capital-labour CES production function was introduced by Solow and popularised by Arrow, Chenery, Minhas and Solow.
Linear (perfect substitutes), Cobb–Douglas and Leontief (perfect complements) functions are special cases of it.
With more than two factors it generally cannot keep a constant elasticity between every pair, as Uzawa showed.
Nested CES functions are common in partial and general equilibrium models, letting each nest carry its own elasticity.
As a utility function, goods are perfect substitutes as the elasticity approaches infinity and perfect complements as it approaches zero.

definition.text: The elasticity of substitution measures how easily one input or good can be swapped for another: the percentage change in their ratio of use for a percentage change in their relative marginal values or prices.

facts.text: Its most common use is the ratio of capital to labour relative to the ratio of their marginal products or prices.
John Hicks introduced it in 1932, and Joan Robinson independently discovered it in 1933.
It measures the curvature of an isoquant; the larger it is, the more readily one input is substituted for another.
Below one, goods are gross complements and relative spending on a good rises with its relative price; above one they are gross substitutes and it falls.
At exactly one, the Cobb–Douglas case, relative spending does not depend on relative prices.

definition.text: The overlapping generations (OLG) model is a leading framework in macroeconomic dynamics in which people live for a finite time, long enough to overlap with other generations.

facts.text: It is the natural framework for studying how resources are allocated across generations, for example through Social Security.
Maurice Allais first formulated it in 1947, Paul Samuelson more rigorously in 1958, and Peter Diamond added production in 1965.
Its steady-state equilibrium need not be efficient, unlike general equilibrium models covered by the first welfare theorem; in Diamond's version people save more than is socially optimal.

definition.text: Critical natural capital is natural capital such as air, water and land whose ecological functions cannot be replaced by human-made alternatives, as opposed to non-critical capital such as minerals.

facts.text: Strong sustainability holds that such critical assets must be maintained regardless of gains in other kinds of capital.
Adjusted net national income subtracts natural resource depletion but does not account for critical natural capital.

title: Substitutability of natural capital

definition.text: Substitutability of natural capital is the question of how far human-made capital (buildings, machinery, technology) can replace natural capital (forests, water, clean air).

facts.text: It is the dividing line of the weak versus strong sustainability debate, argued over ardently since the 1990s.
Solow showed that, given some substitutability, accumulating produced capital fast enough can offset a shrinking exhaustible resource stock.
Solow and Stiglitz both held that across-the-board substitution of man-made for natural capital is a real possibility.
Georgescu-Roegen countered that, since the economic process steadily increases entropy, such across-the-board substitutability is untenable.
William Rees criticises mainstream economics for assuming perfect substitutability between manufactured or financial capital and natural capital.

contested_note: Neoclassical economists such as Solow and Stiglitz and ecological economists such as Georgescu-Roegen disagree on whether substitution is possible.
